What's the status on bringing factories back to the US?

They're probably not coming back in the form we used to imagine. The traditional factory is an anachronism. Most consumer goods are now produced in contract 'job shops'. Corporations are on a long trend of divesting in ownership of production in favor of contract production because the cost of money--the amortized cost of that ownership--is becoming the biggest drag on competitiveness. Production is not only being automated, it's essential nature is changing. The machines are becoming generalist and merging with automated distribution.

So when production returns to the US it will not only be highly automated--hence no restored jobs--, it will be demassified, taking the form of systems distributed across the automated distribution networks, producing goods on-demand instead of speculatively --thus destroying the need for capital. Labor and Capital are on two decks of the same sinking boat. It will become a kind of commodity service or municipal utility. An Internet of Stuff. What futurists call Industry 4.0, or the Fourth Industrial Revolution, or the Post-Industrial era. Production will be everywhere and most goods will be produced, in their final stages at least, close to the point of purchase. Close to home. Cars will be assembled to order at the dealership, or at nearby brand-agnostic car fabs and drive themselves to your home. Appliances and consumer electronics assembled within the network, on the way to being delivered to your house. That's how production will come home.
